quests.ruleExplanation: English statements begin with the subject before the verb: 'The students' (who) comes before 'laugh' (what they do). There is no object here — the verb alone completes the idea.
quests.nativeTip: Find who is doing the laughing, and place that before the action word.

quests.ruleExplanation: Local describes musicians, so it stays directly in front of the noun it modifies, and the whole subject phrase comes before the verb perform.
quests.nativeTip: The word describing the musicians stays attached to them, right before the verb.

quests.ruleExplanation: Even with a longer subject — 'The tall office building' — English keeps the same rule: everything describing the subject comes first, and the verb trembles still comes last.
quests.nativeTip: A longer subject can include several describing words, but the verb still comes after all of them.

quests.ruleExplanation: The chef (subject) performs the action prepares (verb), and dinner (object) is the thing being prepared — the standard S-V-O pattern.
quests.nativeTip: After naming who acts and what they do, add the thing that receives the action.

quests.ruleExplanation: Plural nouns like nurses and patients don't need an article, but the order stays the same: subject, then verb, then object.
quests.nativeTip: A plural subject with no article still comes first, followed by the verb, then the object.

quests.ruleExplanation: New describes manager and stays right before it; the sentence still follows subject + verb + object with reviews contracts completing the action.
quests.nativeTip: Keep the describing word next to the subject noun, then follow with the verb and object.

quests.ruleExplanation: Tastes links soup to the description delicious. Unlike action verbs, linking verbs are followed by a complement that describes the subject, not a separate object.
quests.nativeTip: Tastes is a linking verb here — it connects the subject to a word that describes it, not an object.

quests.ruleExplanation: Her voice is the subject, sounds is the linking verb, and calm describes the voice itself — this is a complement, not something being acted on.
quests.nativeTip: Put the possessor and the thing possessed together first, then the linking verb, then the description.

quests.ruleExplanation: Is is the most common linking verb. This restaurant is the subject, and famous describes it directly through is, following the same S-V-C pattern as tastes and sounds.
quests.nativeTip: Is often works this way too: subject, then is, then the word that describes the subject.

quests.ruleExplanation: I replaces a noun as the subject but the sentence still follows subject + verb + object: I enjoy long walks.
quests.nativeTip: A pronoun subject like I follows the same order as any other subject: it comes first.

quests.ruleExplanation: They is a subject pronoun and needs no article; it goes straight before the verb organize, followed by the object community events.
quests.nativeTip: The pronoun stands alone before the verb — no article or extra word needed with plural pronouns.

quests.ruleExplanation: We is the subject pronoun, appreciate is the verb, and your effort is the object — showing that possessive words like your can appear within the object too.
quests.nativeTip: The subject pronoun leads the sentence, and a possessive word can appear inside the object phrase.

quests.ruleExplanation: An is used before iced because it starts with a vowel sound. The article sits directly before the adjective and noun it introduces: an iced coffee.
quests.nativeTip: Use an, not a, before a word that starts with a vowel sound.

quests.ruleExplanation: A is used before bicycle because it begins with a consonant sound. It stays attached to the noun phrase it introduces: a bicycle helmet.
quests.nativeTip: A goes before a word starting with a consonant sound, right before the noun phrase.

quests.sentence: Our manager finalizes the budget report.
quests.ruleExplanation: Our introduces the subject, and the appears before budget report because it refers to one specific, known report — the definite article the marks something already understood.
quests.nativeTip: A possessive word can open the sentence, while the appears later inside the object phrase.

quests.ruleExplanation: This is a demonstrative that points to one specific neighborhood; it takes the place of an article directly before the noun.
quests.nativeTip: This points to something specific and singular, and it sits right before the noun.

quests.ruleExplanation: That singles out one particular restaurant, likely one already known to the listener, and sits directly before the noun it modifies.
quests.nativeTip: That works like this, but usually refers to something farther away or already mentioned.

quests.ruleExplanation: These agrees with the plural noun options, and the whole phrase seating options acts as one unit after the demonstrative.
quests.nativeTip: These is the plural form of this — it must match a plural noun.

quests.ruleExplanation: My shows the relationship between the speaker and colleague; it functions like an article, sitting directly before the subject noun.
quests.nativeTip: A possessive word shows who owns or relates to the noun, and comes right before it.

quests.ruleExplanation: Their marks the subject as belonging to a group, while honest describes feedback inside the object phrase — both stay right before their nouns.
quests.nativeTip: The possessive word can start the sentence, and a single describing word can sit inside the object phrase.

quests.ruleExplanation: Its is the possessive form used for objects, animals, or machines; here it shows that the engine belongs to something already mentioned, like a car.
quests.nativeTip: Its (no apostrophe) shows possession for a thing, not a person — it still comes right before the noun.

quests.ruleExplanation: Several indicates an unspecified but noticeable number, and it comes before the adjective close and the noun friends, in that order.
quests.nativeTip: A quantifier like several tells us how many, and comes before any describing word and the noun.

quests.sentence: The bakery sells many fresh pastries.
quests.ruleExplanation: Many expresses a large but unspecified quantity, positioned before fresh and pastries, following the same pattern as other quantifiers.
quests.nativeTip: Many also shows quantity and goes in the same slot as several, before the adjective and noun.

quests.sentence: She keeps a few old photographs.
quests.ruleExplanation: A few is a two-word quantifier that functions as a single unit; it stays together before old and photographs, unlike single-word quantifiers such as many.
quests.nativeTip: A few acts as one unit meaning 'some' — keep those two words together before the adjective and noun.

quests.ruleExplanation: Us is an object pronoun that replaces a noun phrase like the players; it takes the same position a full object would, right after the verb.
quests.nativeTip: Object pronouns like us come right after the verb, in the object's usual position.

quests.ruleExplanation: My parents is the subject phrase, and them is the object pronoun replacing a group of people already mentioned, sitting right after the verb.
quests.nativeTip: The subject can be a possessive noun phrase, while the object slot holds a pronoun like them.

quests.sentence: The customer service team calls him.
quests.ruleExplanation: Customer service team is a compound noun acting as one subject unit; the object pronoun him still follows immediately after the verb calls, unaffected by the subject's length.
quests.nativeTip: Even a multi-word subject like a team name doesn't change where the object pronoun goes.

quests.sentence: Our new neighbor walks her small dog.
quests.ruleExplanation: This review sentence layers a possessive and adjective before the subject noun (Our new neighbor) and again before the object noun (her small dog), around the central verb walks.
quests.nativeTip: Combine everything you've learned: possessive + adjective for the subject, then the verb, then possessive + adjective for the object.

quests.sentence: The friendly barista remembers my usual order.
quests.ruleExplanation: The friendly barista uses an article and adjective to build the subject, while my usual order uses a possessive and adjective to build the object, showing how noun phrases grow while the core S-V-O order stays fixed.
quests.nativeTip: Article and adjective build the subject; possessive and adjective build the object — the verb sits between them.

quests.sentence: Several loyal customers recommend this popular bakery.
quests.ruleExplanation: Several loyal customers combines a quantifier and adjective before the subject noun, and this popular bakery combines a demonstrative and adjective before the object noun — a fitting final review of everything from this file.
quests.nativeTip: A quantifier and adjective open the subject; a demonstrative and adjective open the object.
